subject: religious-studies
topicDisplay: Component 3: Issues of Life and Death
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does the term 'sanctity of life' mean?
options: The belief that life is holy and sacred because it is God-given
The belief that life should be as comfortable as possible
The belief that only human life has any value
The belief that life begins at birth
questions.explain: Sanctity of life is the idea that life is precious and sacred because it is created and given by God.

questions.q: Which scientific theory explains the origin of the universe?
options: The Big Bang theory
The theory of natural selection
The steady state of creation
The theory of relativity
questions.explain: The Big Bang theory states the universe began from a single expanding point of dense energy around 13.8 billion years ago.

questions.q: What does the idea of 'stewardship' teach Christians about the world?
options: Humans have a duty to care for and protect the world on God's behalf
Humans may use the world's resources however they wish
The world will look after itself without human help
Only religious people are responsible for the environment
questions.explain: Stewardship, based on Genesis, teaches that God has entrusted humans to look after creation responsibly.

questions.q: In Genesis, humans are described as being made in the 'image of God'. What is the Latin term for this?
options: Imago Dei
Ex nihilo
Agape
Logos
questions.explain: Imago Dei means 'image of God' and expresses the belief that humans uniquely reflect God's nature.

questions.q: A company pollutes a river and harms local wildlife. Which Christian teaching most directly challenges this behaviour?
options: Stewardship
The Big Bang
Purgatory
Voluntary euthanasia
questions.explain: Stewardship holds that humans must protect creation, so damaging the environment goes against this duty.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'quality of life'?
options: The general wellbeing and standard of a person's life
The belief that all life is equally sacred
The total length of a person's life
The amount of medical care a person receives
questions.explain: Quality of life concerns how good, comfortable or worthwhile a person's life is, rather than its mere existence.

questions.q: In which year was the Abortion Act passed, legalising abortion in Great Britain?
questions.explain: The 1967 Abortion Act legalised abortion in Great Britain under certain conditions agreed by two doctors.

questions.q: What is the general legal time limit for most abortions in Great Britain?
options: 24 weeks
12 weeks
28 weeks
40 weeks
questions.explain: Most abortions are legally permitted up to 24 weeks of pregnancy, a limit set by the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990.

questions.q: Which statement best describes voluntary euthanasia?
options: A person makes a clear request for their own life to be ended
A person's life is ended without their knowledge or consent
A person's life is ended because they cannot express any wish
A person recovers naturally from a terminal illness
questions.explain: Voluntary euthanasia is when a person, usually terminally ill, consciously asks for help to end their own life.

questions.q: Why do many Christians oppose abortion?
options: Because life is sacred and given by God from conception
Because it is always against the law
Because it improves the quality of life
Because the Bible commands stewardship of the environment
questions.explain: The sanctity of life principle leads many Christians to argue that ending a life in the womb is wrong.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the 'pro-choice' position on abortion?
options: A woman has the right to choose what happens to her own body
Abortion is wrong in every circumstance
Life is sacred from the moment of conception
Only doctors should decide whether abortion is allowed
questions.explain: The pro-choice view emphasises a woman's right to make decisions about her own body and pregnancy.

questions.q: A terminally ill patient in severe pain asks a doctor to give them a lethal injection to end their suffering. This is an example of?
options: Voluntary euthanasia
Passive euthanasia
Non-voluntary euthanasia
Natural death
questions.explain: The patient is consciously requesting an active end to their life, which defines voluntary euthanasia.

questions.q: Christian belief in life after death is based mainly on which event?
options: The resurrection of Jesus
The parting of the Red Sea
The Big Bang
The Ten Commandments
questions.explain: Christians point to Jesus rising from the dead as evidence and hope for their own life after death.

questions.q: Which group of Christians traditionally believes in purgatory?
options: Roman Catholics
Quakers
Baptists
Methodists
questions.explain: Roman Catholics teach that purgatory is a state of purification before entering heaven, a belief most Protestants reject.

questions.q: In Islam, the belief in life after death is known as?
options: Akhirah
Ummah
Tawhid
Zakat
questions.explain: Akhirah is the Islamic term for the afterlife, where people are judged and sent to Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell).

questions.q: What do Christians mean by 'judgement'?
options: God will assess each person's life and decide their eternal fate
People choose their own religion during their lifetime
The universe judges good and bad actions automatically
Only priests can decide who goes to heaven
questions.explain: Judgement is the belief that God evaluates a person's life and actions, determining whether they go to heaven or hell.

questions.q: A Humanist is asked what they believe happens after death. Which answer best fits their view?
options: Nothing survives death; a person simply ceases to exist
The soul is reborn into a new body
The person is judged by God and sent to heaven or hell
The person waits in purgatory before entering paradise
questions.explain: Humanists reject belief in a soul or afterlife, holding that death is the end of a person's existence.

questions.q: Why do some people refer to near-death experiences when discussing life after death?
options: As possible evidence that life continues after death
As proof that the Big Bang created the universe
To argue that abortion should be legal
To show that stewardship is a religious duty
questions.explain: Reports of near-death experiences are sometimes used to suggest that consciousness may survive bodily death.

questions.q: How do many Christians respond to the scientific account of the universe's origin?
options: They accept the Big Bang as the method God used to create the universe
They insist science and religion can never agree
They reject all scientific evidence about the universe
They believe the universe has always existed unchanged
questions.explain: Many Christians see no conflict, viewing the Big Bang as the process through which God brought about creation.

questions.q: In which situation are some Christians most likely to accept that abortion may be permissible?
options: When the mother's life is at serious risk
When the child is an inconvenience
Whenever the mother changes her mind
When the family wants a different gender
questions.explain: Although many Christians oppose abortion, some accept it as the lesser of two evils when the mother's life is endangered.
